# Checkpoint 77: normal Jak II runtime completes its first bounded display tick

Date: 2026-08-03. Nested commit
`b0db0d9f1251bbbfae2e1919bff2e276a77796d7` closes the three failures exposed
while moving Checkpoint 76's bounded Metal presenter into the normal Jak II
runtime path. It does not yet render a title-screen pixel or establish Jak II
gameplay.

## Crash sequence and fixes

The maintainer's original simulator report is from bundle
`com.zephyrstudiosllc.eco.jak2dev`, UUID
`C4C72D06-585E-32F3-A95B-F40D12E2A4DA`. It faulted at PC zero from
`goal_main_display_loop + 744`; the live register state had `x8=0` and the
suspend-hook GOAL object in `x9=#x001c7fb4`. Nested commits `56c29df60` and
`cc8c4e217` add a product-linked live suspend-hook probe and guard every
generated indirect `GOAL_FN` call. A corrupt or out-of-range native entry now
logs the generated source location, GOAL object, and current process before
aborting instead of executing `blr 0`. Focused death tests cover both a zero
entry and a function object below the protected GOAL-memory boundary.

The rebuilt source pack showed the same `#x001c7fb4` suspend-hook object with a
valid native entry. That exposed the next failure in PC settings: the former
`pc-filepath-exists?` stub returned C zero, which is not GOAL false, and the
former `file-stream-open` stub also returned zero. Generated settings code then
treated the failed open as valid and read `g_goal_mem + 0xc`. Nested commit
`a2ee5729d` implements the narrow Jak II portable file-stream, settings-path,
and display-query seams. Settings stay inside the app sandbox at
`Library/Application Support/OpenGOAL/jak2/settings`. The focused machine test
now covers stream round-trip, missing-file behavior, sign-extended failure,
settings globals, and PC query functions.

The next run reached `time-of-day` and tripped the GOAL thread stack invariant:
the live function used 976 bytes against an 896-byte converted backup. The
iPhoneOS-only CMake generator returns before the repository's global Release
optimization defaults, so Xcode had compiled the generated AOT corpus at
`-O0`. Nested commit `b0db0d9f1` applies target-local
`-O3 -fno-strict-aliasing` to that corpus. A clean rebuild reduced
`goal_time_of_day_anon_function_1` to a `0xa0`-byte native frame and the same
runtime path passed without enlarging GOAL's stack constants.

# Build 84: emulate OpenGL D24 quantization for Metal backgrounds

Date: 2026-08-04. This candidate restarts from the exact physical known-best
Build 79 parent `c2e4d12a0f656f898587690935beaeb81debe6a6` and its OpenGOAL
gitlink `816222f47c715e770a789a29830c66634af880d9`. It does not contain
Build 81's anisotropy experiment, Build 82's texture-sampling bypass, or Build
83's camera-relative ETIE projection change.

Build 83 was physically rejected after an explicitly authorized install and
launch on Z iPad Pro. Camera stability regressed to an unacceptable state, and
the Precursor-metal flicker did not change from Build 79. That falsifies the
camera-relative ETIE evaluation-order hypothesis for this symptom. Build 84
therefore preserves Build 79's camera and projection math.

## D24/D32 proof and production scope

The desktop OpenGL renderer requests 24 depth bits and creates
`GL_DEPTH24_STENCIL8`. The iPad Metal renderer uses
`MTLPixelFormatDepth32Float_Stencil8`; Metal's native
`MTLPixelFormatDepth24Unorm_Stencil8` is unavailable on iOS. Reviewed proof
commit `74e5944d5c3493b73cf9442a9a81fe99548f6d19` adds a synthetic,
asset-free GPU readback that runs the real TFRAG3 and ETIE-base vertex paths at
native D32 precision and with fragment-stage D24 quantization. Across nearby
camera positions it demonstrates distinct D32 values collapsing into one D24
bin: native reversed-depth `GEQUAL` rejects the slightly farther ETIE base,
while equalized D24 depth lets that pass win. The proof retains a byte-identical
D32 camera A/B/A control.

Production commit `5a1422e4d4a75729570084fed1f93a8ebd56d6c5` shares the proof's
fixed-depth conversion in `tfrag3_fs`:

```text
round(clamp(depth, 0, 1) * 16777215) / 16777215
```

That fragment entry point is used by ordinary TFRAG3, the envmapped TIE base,
and the reflective ETIE draw. The backing depth/stencil target remains D32/S8;
only the depth value written by those background fragments is quantized. A
production-path readback matches the proof quantizer, equalized depth preserves
the intended `GEQUAL` result, and an adjacent-bin negative control remains
distinct. Camera math, vertex projection, texture/sampler behavior, draw order,
visibility, fog/color math, blend state, depth compare/write policy, Merc,
shrubs, sprites, Generic2, ocean, shadows, Swift/Objective-C++, and AOT output
are unchanged.

This is a narrow parity candidate, not a physical visual fix claim. Explicit
fragment depth can reduce early-depth optimization, and its performance and
visual effect remain pending on physical hardware.

### Physical verdict

The maintainer completed the Build 84 comparison on Z iPad Pro. Build 84 had
the least metallic-material flicker of any candidate so far: lamps and other
metal surfaces flickered roughly three to five times while walking past them,
instead of roughly one hundred times in the earlier behavior. Precursor
surfaces remained visibly chunked and still changed about three times per
second, but this was also a large reduction from the earlier rapid flicker.
No regression was observed in the previously fixed camera, Jak transform,
Merc deformation, movement, or attack behavior.

Build 84 is not acceptable as the final build because physical performance
regressed from Build 79's steady, cool approximately 60 fps behavior to
noticeable drops near 30 and 15 fps, and the iPad became warm. This matches the
known risk of an explicit fragment-stage `[[depth(any)]]` write reducing early
depth rejection on Apple's tile renderer. Treat Build 84 as the best visual
candidate and proof that D24-equivalent background depth addresses the correct
defect; keep Build 79 as the overall performance baseline. The next candidate
must preserve the D24 visual improvement while avoiding the unrestricted
fragment-depth path, eliminate the remaining chunking/flicker, and leave all
camera, Jak, Merc, input, timing, and gameplay code unchanged.

During a later Build 84 run, the maintainer also observed a camera regression
that had not been apparent in the first comparison. Build 84 is therefore
rejected for camera stability as well as performance and residual flicker. Do
not reinterpret the earlier initial no-regression observation as final
acceptance.

# Build 85: invariant ETIE rasterizer depth without fragment-depth writes

Date: 2026-08-04. Build 85 keeps Build 79's camera, projection, gameplay, Merc,
input, and renderer state while replacing Build 84's global fragment-stage D24
write. Production `tfrag3_fs` is color-only again, so ordinary TFRAG3,
ETIE_BASE, and ETIE return to normal rasterizer depth and retain early depth
testing on Apple's tile renderer. `BackgroundVSOut.pos` is now
`[[position, invariant]]`, and every first-party Metal compiler invocation uses
`-fpreserve-invariance`. The ETIE base and reflective passes therefore receive
bit-identical rasterizer positions and depth without an unrestricted
per-fragment depth export. Build-local module caches avoid dependence on the
user-global clang cache in both CMake and Xcode.

after Build 86 investigation began. Preserve these isolated worktrees:

  `agent/build86-metal-perf-parent`, created from the Build 85 physical-verdict

No Build 86 production source has been edited yet. The leading performance
hypothesis is the shared `BackgroundVSOut.pos [[position, invariant]]`. It marks
all four `tfrag3_vs`, `etie_base_vs`, `etie_vs`, and `shrub_vs` position
outputs invariant. Apple's documented preserve-invariance behavior applies the
conservative compilation to marked position outputs, not automatically to
every unmarked shader in the same command. Beach frame 1838 contains about
220,485 background triangles but only 714 reflective ETIE triangles; Geyser's
movement-start frame similarly has about 80,000 background triangles but only
630 reflective triangles. Build 85 therefore pays the invariance cost across
nearly all high-volume world and vegetation vertex work to repair a sub-one-
percent paired-pass seam. This is the narrowest source-level difference capable
of explaining its physical heat/frame regression after the fragment-depth
write was removed.

## Selective AIR toolchain proof

The Apple Metal driver can compile individual source files with different
flags and link the AIR outputs into one metallib. The primary lane verified the
mechanism against current repository shaders:

```sh
xcrun -sdk macosx metal -Wall -Werror -c \
  -fmodules-cache-path=/private/tmp/goalpad-build86-air-proof/module-cache \
  game/graphics/pipelines/metal/shaders/scaffold.metal \
  -o /private/tmp/goalpad-build86-air-proof/scaffold.air
xcrun -sdk macosx metal -Wall -Werror -fpreserve-invariance -c \
  -fmodules-cache-path=/private/tmp/goalpad-build86-air-proof/module-cache \
  game/graphics/pipelines/metal/shaders/background.metal \
  -o /private/tmp/goalpad-build86-air-proof/background.air
xcrun -sdk macosx metal \
  /private/tmp/goalpad-build86-air-proof/scaffold.air \
  /private/tmp/goalpad-build86-air-proof/background.air \
  -o /private/tmp/goalpad-build86-air-proof/scoped.metallib
```

Both AIR compilations and the final link passed. A separate synthetic audit
also compiled a normal base AIR and an invariant ETIE AIR, linked them with a
shared fragment function, and confirmed `base_vs`, `etie_vs`, and `shared_fs`
in one library. The driver cannot use one `-o` for multiple `-c` inputs, so the
fallback selective build would need to emit one AIR per `.metal` file and link
them afterward. The
standalone `metallib` utility is not exposed by this Xcode installation;
`xcrun -sdk <sdk> metal <air...> -o <library>` is the validated link command.

## Next executable Build 86 task

Keep both ETIE vertex stages together in one preserved translation unit; making
only the reflective stage invariant is insufficient. The smallest candidate
does not yet require a source-file or build-system split:

1. Restore `BackgroundVSOut.pos` to ordinary `[[position]]`.
2. Add a field-for-field identical `InvariantEtieVSOut` whose position alone is
   `[[position, invariant]]`.
3. Change only `etie_base_vs` and `etie_vs` to return and populate
   `InvariantEtieVSOut`; leave TFRAG3 and shrub on `BackgroundVSOut`.
4. Keep the existing `-fpreserve-invariance` compile commands. If Metal rejects

   than weakening invariance; the already-proven separate-AIR/source split is
   the fallback.
5. First run changed-file Metal compilation and the 65-camera invariant proof.

### Physical performance verdict

The maintainer physically tested the installed Build 86 and reported that it
felt just as frame-dippy as Build 85. Build 86 is therefore rejected as a
performance improvement. This verdict is specific to performance; do not infer
a new visual or gameplay verdict that the maintainer did not report.

The result falsifies the hypothesis that removing invariant output from only
TFRAG3 and shrub would materially restore Build 79's performance. The exact
Build 79-to-Build 86 production render delta is now especially narrow:

- Build 84's explicit fragment-depth write is not present in Build 85 or 86.
- Build 86 leaves `[[position, invariant]]` only on `etie_base_vs` and
  `etie_vs`.
- The entire Metal shader library is still compiled with
  `-fpreserve-invariance`; Build 79 was not.

Apple documents that preserve-invariance compiles a vertex shader
conservatively when its position output is marked invariant. A mere selective
AIR split would therefore be unlikely to change Build 86's remaining ETIE
cost. The narrow next production direction is to make ETIE base and shine use
one vertex entry point whose position calculation is necessarily identical,
then remove both the invariant marker and preserve-invariance compiler flag.
That should retain the solved paired-pass coverage without any conservative
vertex compilation. It must pass the existing 65-camera ETIE coverage/depth
proof and frozen Build 85 pixel comparisons before another signed build.

# Build 87 shared-ETIE release candidate

Date: 2026-08-04. Build 87 is the direct follow-up to Build 86's physical
performance rejection. It removes invariant compilation entirely rather than
trying another compiler-scope variation.

The isolated worktrees are:

- Parent: `/private/tmp/GP-build87-shared-etie-parent`, branch
  `agent/build87-shared-etie-parent`.
- Child: `/private/tmp/OG-build87-shared-etie`, branch
  `agent/build87-shared-etie`, commit
  `a9e764545a86dd624dae9248254f4f7a470e2ce3`.
- The parent integration commit before this handoff update is
  `63292b830334cd1013427ce3487ad5f9a4a538e1` and points at that exact child.

Both ETIE pipeline-state IDs now use one `etie_shared_vs` vertex entry point.
It completes the shared position calculation before a uniform `etie_shine`
branch changes only fog, color, and UV output. The existing 16-byte draw
parameter ABI now carries `decal`, `etie_shine`, and two padding words. The
base and shine PSOs remain separate because their blend/depth state differs.
The old `[[position, invariant]]` output and `-fpreserve-invariance` compiler
flag were removed from both the CMake Metal product and Xcode shader script.

This design follows Apple's documented role for
[`preserveInvariance`](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/metal/mtlcompileoptions/preserveinvariance):
the conservative compilation applies to marked vertex-position output. Apple
also recommends invariance for paired passes that require identical positions
in its
[`Porting your Metal code to Apple silicon`](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/apple-silicon/porting-your-metal-code-to-apple-silicon)
guidance. Reusing one entry point is not documented as a formal invariance
guarantee, so the deterministic GPU proof and physical result remain the
authority for this narrower implementation.

## Build 87 physical acceptance gate

On 2026-08-04, the maintainer explicitly authorized putting Build 87 on
`Z iPad Pro` (`6A4111AB-1663-508A-98D9-F0C1A9EA7863`). The preserved app was
installed in place with `devicectl`, preserving the existing app data
container. Device-side app inspection confirmed Eco Pro `1.0 (87)`, bundle
identifier `com.zephyrstudiosllc.eco`. The maintainer then explicitly
authorized launch, and `devicectl` successfully launched that bundle
identifier. No device logs or screen capture were requested or collected.

Build 87 is implemented, build-validated, and installed, but it is not accepted
until the maintainer confirms both gates on the physical device:

1. Build 85 visual/gameplay behavior remains intact: no reflective flicker or
   chunking and no camera, Jak, Merc, movement, attack, or gameplay regression.
2. Sustained smoothness, frame pacing, and heat restore or exceed Build 79.

Build 79 remains the performance baseline, Build 85 remains the solved
visual/gameplay baseline, and Build 86 remains a rejected performance
candidate. Do not claim Build 87 improves performance from static proofs or a
generic signed build alone.

the narrow follow-up is a separate diagnostics-off A/B, starting with the
scheduled atomic snapshot rather than removing renderer correctness counters.

## Build 88 physical performance verdict

The maintainer and a second independent tester physically tested the cold-
launched Build 88. The device was noticeably cooler than Builds 85/86 and did
not become warm. Jak still felt smooth and responsive to control. This is
evidence that removing conservative invariant compilation materially reduced
the sustained GPU/thermal cost.

Build 88 is nevertheless rejected as the final performance fix. Both testers
noticed a regular single-frame-looking hitch: approximately one event every
30-60 frames or around once per second, described as a stutter that can feel
loosely synchronized with footsteps. The action remains responsive while the
presented motion is not consistently smooth. The maintainer did not provide a
new explicit reflective-flicker, camera, Merc, or other visual-correctness
verdict in this report; do not infer one.

Treat thermal load and frame pacing as separate results. Build 88 is the
current cool shared-ETIE candidate, but Build 79 remains the accepted smoothness
baseline and Build 85 remains the solved visual/gameplay baseline. The next
task is to distinguish an actual CADisplayLink/presentation miss from a
simulation/camera cadence jump or scheduled diagnostic I/O before changing
renderer behavior again.

## Next enhancement gates

The Build 89 touch implementation is already newer than the preexisting
README/BUILDING description. Its first left-half contact creates a dynamic
movement-stick origin; a fixed bottom-right control emits a continuous analog R
stick; right-half swipes emit Cross, Square, Circle, or held L1; reversing an L1
swipe upward adds Cross; and short taps are inert. The documentation in this
acceptance commit is corrected to match that code. Deterministic touch checks
pass, but no current physical multitouch, latency, or ergonomic verdict is
recorded.

The previously proposed Enhanced-touch candidate is deferred. Per maintainer
direction, no touch source changes belong in the current settings/Hor+ work.
The next physical gate is Classic versus Graphics Modern Fill Width; the touch
contract remains a later product decision.

The existing shared app already includes `xros` and `xrsimulator`, uses a normal
SwiftUI `WindowGroup` backed by one `CAMetalLayer`, and leaves gameplay
controller-only on visionOS. Build 90 adds a generic visionOS Release compile,
but physical runtime evidence is not recorded. The smallest Apple Vision Pro
slice remains physical validation of the conventional Classic Mode window with
prepared data, controller, Metal, audio, and lifecycle smoke. Do not add
immersive presentation, stereo rendering, RealityKit, spatial input, or
multiwindow architecture to that first slice.

# Build 90 Modern/Classic settings and Hor+ candidate

Date: 2026-08-04. Work continues in
`/private/tmp/GP-modern-mode-horplus` on branch
`agent/modern-mode-horplus`. Build 89 remains locked and tagged as the canonical
Classic Mode baseline; its worktree, signed app, and tags were not modified.
No touch-control source changed.

The settings shell now has independent Controls, Graphics, Audio, and UI
Classic/Modern profiles, per-section Restore Defaults, a Mixed-aware global
preset, and Reset All. Classic is the all-section default. Option values survive
profile and global-preset changes. Graphics Modern defaults Fill Width (Hor+)
on, while Graphics Classic always keeps it off. Settings persist as one
versioned local JSON document and sync as a separate iCloud document by default.
The iCloud settings opt-out is device-local and does not alter iCloud save sync.

The cloud path coordinates the nearest existing ancestor for its first write,
includes unresolved `NSFileVersion` documents in its timestamp/writer-ID merge,
and resolves them after publishing the winner. Settings preparation is started
alongside save preparation so an iCloud settings download cannot delay the save
gate. A mid-sync device opt-out stops the pending cloud write.

Hor+ is isolated behind the effective Graphics Modern setting. Classic retains
the exact 4:3 target and letterbox arithmetic. Its portable GOAL display query
is disabled by default and reports through the preexisting machine-stub behavior;
only Hor+ enables the live display aspect. On wide drawables Hor+ preserves
internal height, widens the target, fills the drawable, and supplies the wide
aspect to GOAL. Portrait and narrower drawables never narrow the Classic view.

# ProMotion / 120 Hz effort research

Date: 2026-08-05. Read-only research confirmed the current iPad frame loop is
hard-capped to 60 Hz in `GameSurfaceView.swift`. Every display-link callback
runs one full dispatcher frame, one sound frame, input, renderer submission,
and presentation. `GOALPadDisplayClock` also converts elapsed timestamps with a
fixed `* 60.0` calculation. Raising only the display-link range to 120 would
therefore attempt roughly 120 ordinary 60 Hz simulation steps each second; it
would not be a correct high-refresh presentation mode.

OpenGOAL contains useful custom-FPS groundwork, including 120-FPS pad history,
but 120 exposes a concrete timing gap: the custom display time factor is
`300 / target-fps`, or 2.5 at 120, while `drawable.gc` converts the value to an
integer for several counters. The iPad boot path also does not currently own a
GOAL target-FPS configuration seam. Audio maintenance and fades run once per
dispatcher frame, and the Metal renderer waits synchronously for the previous
command buffer before reusing stream pages. These require explicit timing and
throughput validation rather than a plist or display-link-only change.

Apple documents ProMotion as a best-effort range rather than a forced rate.
iPad Pro may dynamically select 120, 60, 40, 30, or 24 Hz, and callbacks must
use `targetTimestamp` and recover from missed intervals. iPad Pro does not need
the iPhone-only `CADisableMinimumFrameDurationOnPhone` key.

Estimated effort for a credible experimental mode is two to four weeks:

1. One to two days for a boot-only 60/120 setting, timing instrumentation, and
   deterministic 120/60/40/30/24 callback traces. This is a spike, not a
   shippable mode.
2. One to two weeks for an app-owned AOT frame-rate seam, correct fractional
   time accumulation, fallback cadence behavior, and audio/input timing tests.
3. Three to five days for signed-device A/B validation and tuning at 1x, then
   2x internal resolution.
4. A conditional additional one to two or more weeks if physical measurements
   require replacing the renderer's single in-flight stream ownership model.

The smallest useful physical proof is a 30-second 60-versus-120 A/B of one
scene at 1x resolution, recording actual target-timestamp intervals, dispatcher
frames, cumulative game time, submitted/presented/late frames, and prior-command
buffer waits. A valid result must sustain approximately 8.33 ms callbacks while
game time, camera, input, timers, audio fades, and dialogue duration remain
correct. No 120 Hz code was implemented and no physical ProMotion test was run.

# Misty transition diagnosis after Build 104

Date: 2026-08-06. Root and three read-only Sol/Terra lanes separated the
destination's steady state from the boat transition before starting fixes.

- Build 90 and Build 93 use the identical OpenGOAL commit `bcc4ee8e`; the
  Build 90-to-93 parent delta contains no renderer, shader, Metal host, AOT, or
  generated-source change. The failure is therefore treated as an unvisited
  transition gap, not an iCloud regression.
- Root configured `/private/tmp/GOALPad-misty-diagnosis-cmake` from the exact
  integration child with Release, Ninja, `BUILD_TESTING=ON`, and ccache, then
  built `jak1-data-boot-test` successfully.
- A 5000-frame direct `misty-start` run against the maintainer's local prepared
  Jak 1 data passed. `MIS.DGO` loaded, all Misty code/data linked through the
  AOT path, `misty-vis` logged in, Misty reached `'active`, and the target
  remained in a stable stance. This is not physical-device or boat-sequence
  proof.
- Root built `goalpad-play` and ran the same direct route through Metal. The
  loader reported 627 textures, 73.2 MB of Misty vertices, 10.1 MB of Misty
  indices, zero failures, and resident Village1 plus Misty after the desktop
  host evicted title art after 181 unwanted frames. Screenshots
  `/private/tmp/GOALPad-misty-direct-1300.png` and
  `/private/tmp/GOALPad-misty-direct-1600.png` show intact Misty geometry,
  textures, Jak, Daxter, collision, and lighting.
- The strongest iOS-specific cause is now parent Metal resource lifetime. The
  app host never evicts visited level art, while the desktop Metal host does.
  Nested FR3 loading can also accept nil Metal buffers or zero texture handles
  as success, allowing partially allocated geometry to be recorded as loaded
  after a long session.
- A separate loader bug is confirmed: C++ reports a terminal DGO archive error,
  but GOAL maps it to the same `#f` as pending. A level can remain `'loading`
  forever while a `:wait-for-load #f` transition continues without its BSP and
  collision. The actual physical Build 93 DGO result remains unknown because
  no device log or container inspection was authorized in this run.

The maintainer also reported a potentially related transition-state symptom:
after collecting enough power cells, the Fire Canyon staircase camera preview
displayed the large `FIRE CANYON` title before Jak physically entered, and it
cleared only after pause/unpause and additional time. Local source shows that
the authored preview camera can cross non-player Fire Canyon display boundaries
and ambient collection is camera/ear-position based. Do not call this a port
regression until compared with original behavior, but keep it in the same
transition-state test route.

# Build 118 physical rejection and Build 119/120 MVP direction

Date: 2026-08-06. The maintainer physically accepted Fit to Screen in Build
118, but rejected Build 118 as an MVP baseline for two independent regressions:

- Ordinary gameplay touch has been materially broken for several builds. The
  maintainer wants its foundational layout and handling restored to Build 96
  and then frozen while retaining the later bounded touch additions.
- Leaving/backgrounding Eco and resuming can loop a black screen with the theme
  song while the SwiftUI/touch shell remains responsive. This is a native
  lifecycle failure, not an app-shell success.

The maintainer also explicitly scrapped the entire Classic touch concept. Build
119 must provide the Build 96 stick geometry, two-pill layout, and base gesture
handling; retain crouch-left punch, pinch, contextual SKIP, touch haptics,
full-screen warp capture, and Build 118's native-menu
Start/Pause/Resume/Back/Done additions; remove the Controls Modern/Classic picker
and touch-layout editor/runtime effect; and retain old synced documents only for
decode compatibility. Primary Controller, physical-controller bindings,
mouse/keyboard bindings, Graphics Modern/Classic, and accepted Fit to Screen are
separate and remain.

The existing isolated lifecycle work at `/private/tmp/GP-build118-background-recovery`
(`ae399b3e`, `804cfaf1`) is being rebased and audited against the reported black-
screen/theme-loop symptom for Build 120 if it should remain separate. Do not
claim it from deterministic lifecycle tests alone; physical background/lock and
resume must show native frames and audio continuing from the active run.

After the Build 119/120 MVP recovery, stop expanding nonessential iOS settings
or touch features. Audit only actual TestFlight/App Store blockers, then
prioritize true stereoscopic visionOS rendering with Comfort/Normal preserved as
fallback. Build 118 remains preserved evidence, not the release baseline.

## Build 122 physical rejection: gameplay touch is starved

The maintainer rejected Build 122 after reaching gameplay. The controls mostly
look correct, but ordinary one-finger walking, jumping, Pause, and camera input
normally do nothing. Spamming five fingers in a way no player would naturally
use can occasionally produce one movement, kick, or camera sample only about
once every several seconds. This rules out a mere label, mapping, or pulse-length
problem and points at touch-stream ownership before `TouchControls.began`.

Build 96 had one gameplay owner: the UIKit `TouchSurfaceView`. Commit
`31d6c62b` later added a root `DragGesture(minimumDistance: 0)` solely to reclaim
touch chrome after physical-input suppression. That SwiftUI gesture observes the
same full-screen streams as the embedded UIKit view and is the narrow behavioral
difference consistent with the physical starvation. Build 123 must remove that
competing root gesture and call the existing recovery closure from
`TouchSurfaceView.touchesBegan` before mapping those same UIKit touches. Keep the
semantic title/native-menu buttons, intentional menu/warp swipe gestures, and
the physically accepted right-camera geometry unchanged.

and a poison-after-capture equivalence oracle. Production stays synchronous until
that oracle proves the renderer no longer reads live mutable state after capture.

## visionOS stereoscopic Jak 1 acceptance contract

The requested first visionOS product slice is deliberately narrower than the
later tabletop, room-scale, and first-person ideas:

- Launch Eco on Apple Vision Pro, load the user's already prepared Jak 1 data,
  and provide the same Jak 1 gameplay experience as the accepted conventional
  app, presented as true stereoscopic 3D in the game window.
- Preserve Comfort/monoscopic presentation as the fail-closed fallback until
  stereo is proven. Do not describe synthetic, side-by-side, or generic xros
  build evidence as playable physical stereo.
- The stereoscopic mode must remain entirely in visionOS Shared Space as an
  ordinary bounded spatial window: conceptually a floating 3D television. Do
  not open an `ImmersiveSpace`, start ARKit/world tracking, query headset pose,
  drive Jak's camera from head motion, or take over the user's surroundings.
- Produce the stereoscopic pair only from Jak's existing third-person game
  camera and present the appropriate image to each eye on the RealityKit window
  surface, like a 3D movie or other fixed-camera flat-to-stereo game. Other apps
  and windows must remain available. A future volume, tabletop, room-scale, or
  immersive mode is separate work and must not leak into this slice.
- visionOS gameplay is controller-only. Support ordinary gamepads through Eco's
  existing Apple Game Controller path. Disable the gameplay-touch system
  entirely on visionOS: do not create or expose sticks, Pause/Stats/Zoom pills,
  face buttons, swipe hints, contextual touch prompts, or invisible touch hit
  regions. Preserve the accepted iOS touch path exactly.
- When no supported controller is connected, show a top ornament whose exact
  text is `No controller detected.` The text should use the requested purple,
  shimmering treatment without harming readability or accessibility.
- The ornament disappears promptly when a supported controller connects and
  returns promptly on disconnect. Controller presence changes presentation only;
  it must not invent input, stall the runtime, or change iOS controller/touch
  behavior.

The no-controller ornament is the sole app-owned gameplay overlay exception on
visionOS. With a controller connected, the game presentation must be visually
clean; native content rendered by Jak itself is unaffected.

The maintainer explicitly removed Zephyr Flight Sim reference work, PS VR2
Sense support, spatial-controller profiles, and accessory tracking from this
slice. Do not spend time on those paths.

## First-interaction presentation investigation

The maintainer reported that an NPC interaction can show ordinary `STATS` and
Zoom the first time but `SKIP`/`PAUSE` on a repeat, and separately questioned
whether the Muse interaction's Circle prompt appeared. A read-only trace found
two distinct native policies:

- First-introduction versus repeat-reminder SKIP behavior is currently authored
  GOAL policy. Common `play-anim!` entry resets `skippable`; several Sandover NPC
  introduction/hint branches do not set it, while reminder branches do. The
  cutscene bridge exposes the first valid SKIP publication immediately, so a
  Swift retention workaround would be incorrect.
- Face-prompt publication intentionally returns invalid for one frame when a new
  owner/mask first appears, then accepts the same-owner heartbeat. This can omit
  Circle for one deterministic frame but is separate from the authored SKIP
  policy.

Next executable work after the context reset:

1. Review the presentation worker's focused evidence and reject any Swift patch
   that overrides native SKIP truth.
2. Decide and implement the narrowest authored policy that makes eligible first
   NPC introductions skippable, with source-contract coverage, while leaving

3. Separately evaluate whether the face-prompt reader can safely expose its first
   structurally valid seqlock publication immediately; cover first owner, owner
   changes, stale generations, and heartbeat behavior deterministically.

It leaves Comfort rendering unchanged. Stereo now fits each eye within the

`internalHeight`) while preserving the window aspect, instead of rendering two

## 2026-08-09 Build 153 proof-gated stereo candidate

Build 153 is compiled and signed but has not been installed or launched on
Vision Pro. The accepted Build 151 Comfort/2D behavior remains the fallback and
the Build 152 physical stereo rejection remains the baseline.

The proof-first reset produced these local integration commits:

```text
OpenGOAL 220447711 test(metal): diagnose reversed-Z stereo disparity (AI-assisted)
parent   06bf98ae test(visionos): diagnose reversed-Z stereo disparity (AI-assisted)
OpenGOAL 4ff596845 fix(metal): submit stereo pair on one command buffer
parent   abc0e382 fix(visionos): drive stereo with paired LowLevelTextures
OpenGOAL 1058dc944 test(metal): add stereo physical candidate markers (AI-assisted)
parent   4deed2a0 test(visionos): stage stereo physical candidate (AI-assisted)
OpenGOAL 1c2eae29a test(metal): account for rasterized stereo coverage
parent   28fcbcf5 build: stage Eco 153 stereo proof candidate
```

The product stereo surface now binds two stable `LowLevelTexture` resources to
the existing CameraIndex ShaderGraph once. A RealityKit rendering system is the
sole producer. Each scheduled 60 Hz game tick reserves native stream storage
without waiting, lazily acquires both texture replacements, encodes both eye
passes onto one caller-owned Metal command buffer, and commits once without a
CPU/GPU completion wait. Six consecutive busy updates, the first native error,
or 250 ms without a RealityKit rendering heartbeat fails closed to Comfort.
Stalled external stream pages are quarantined before Comfort resumes so stereo
cannot leave the ordinary renderer waiting on them. Normal Stereo/Comfort
toggles do not permanently disable later stereo activation.

The reversed-Z transform is now explicit:

```text
x' = x + eyeSlope * (z - convergenceDepth * w)
delta NDC = S * (d - c)
delta pixels = S * (d - c) * width / 2
```

Build 152 used `S = 0.025`, `c = 0`, which yielded only about 0.4 px of
separation at five meters in a 640-pixel eye image. Build 153 deliberately uses
the existing bounded maximum `S = 0.05` and `c = 0.05`, approximately the Jak 1
five-meter reversed-Z depth. At one meter this is 3.196 mathematical pixels at
640 width; the hard-edged GPU fixture deterministically rasterizes it to 4 px.
This is a physical diagnostic candidate, not a comfort calibration.

The Build 153 artifact also enables temporary per-eye routing markers inside
the completed eye textures, after both game encodes and before the same command
buffer commit. The left texture has a magenta 3x16 vertical tick and the right
texture a cyan 16x3 horizontal tick, both inset 14 px. The code defaults off and
was enabled only for this artifact with:

```text
OTHER_CPLUSPLUSFLAGS='$(inherited) -DGOALPAD_VISION_STEREO_EYE_MARKERS=1'
```

# 2026-08-09 Build 155 installed-data and cloud-save UX checkpoint

Build 154 remains the protected accepted 2D baseline. The maintainer reported
that Build 154 otherwise looks good, but rejected its launcher and cloud-save
behavior: a previously imported and played Jak 1 install could appear as
`Preparing` or request another import until Recheck; save preparation had no
specific launcher explanation; iPhone cloud saves did not behave like the same
build on iPad and Vision Pro; and the combined Sync action appeared inert.

Build 155 is a focused Swift launcher/save correction above that checkpoint:

```text
f8b9d2b5 fix: make installed game readiness deterministic (AI-assisted)
63bf4a62 fix(saves): bound cloud preparation and retry identity changes
3e04a160 build: stage Dark Eco 155 launcher and cloud fixes
```

The launcher now starts with `Checking Local Data` instead of treating an
unchecked install as empty. Active imports alone open the import/setup flow.
Local inspection and pregame save phases have distinct labels, overlapping
inspections publish and return only the newest report, and apparently missing
data is re-inspected before any import offer. A valid installed title therefore
cannot be routed to reimport merely because saves are preparing.

Save startup, save-sync enable, and iCloud identity changes now share one
controller-owned automatic task. A completed launch-time bidirectional sync
satisfies the next Play request instead of being repeated. Play bounds ordinary
cloud preparation to eight seconds, cancels owned cloud work on timeout, allows
one second for its exclusive engine lease to release, and checks the durable
local recovery journal before using native local saves. If the lease does not
release or the journal is unsafe, Play fails visibly rather than overlapping a
cloud replacement with gameplay. One placeholder download poll is bounded to
five seconds. Active gameplay remains upload-only.

Manual combined Sync starts enabled settings and save domains concurrently, so
settings-cloud latency cannot starve save sync. Save unavailability distinguishes
an unavailable account/iCloud Drive from a container that is not ready, gives a

# 2026-08-10 Build 158 truthful cross-device save-sync checkpoint

The maintainer reported that iPad and iPhone could each claim `Up to date` with
recent-looking timestamps while the iPhone still exposed an older Jak 1 save
(85 percent instead of 87 percent). The same iPhone had completed one earlier
cross-device sync, so this checkpoint treats the failure as intermittent cloud
inventory/reconciliation rather than a permanent account or entitlement
failure. Build 157's accepted touch and launcher behavior is otherwise
unchanged.

Build 158 closes four false-success paths:

- A bounded `NSMetadataQuery` initial gather now establishes the iCloud
  Documents inventory before reconciliation. The engine unions those results
  with locally visible files instead of treating a temporarily incomplete
  directory enumeration as an empty cloud store. Discovery failure or timeout
  fails visibly before a local save can be presented as synchronized.
- Active gameplay remains upload-only, but it will not overwrite a remotely
  changed or deterministically newer slot. It defers that cloud winner and
  requires a later bidirectional Library sync. A locally advanced slot still
  uploads during gameplay.
- A coordinated iCloud write is no longer sufficient for a success claim. The
  engine reads the provider's asynchronous upload state after coordination and
  reports `Waiting for iCloud to finish uploading saves` while any written
  ubiquitous item remains pending.
- Settings and saves retain separate summaries and `Last settings sync` / `Last
  saves sync` dates. An empty authoritative inventory says `No saves found on
  this device or in iCloud`, and deferred/pending work cannot publish a new save
  success date. While a game is active the action is explicitly `Upload Saves`
  or `Sync Settings & Upload Saves`; opening Settings no longer launches the
  unrelated preserved-save scan that could invisibly disable the sync action.

The existing pair journal, compare-and-swap checks, conflict preservation,
import/export behavior, and cloud-unavailable local authority remain in place.
Apple does not expose a global cross-device strong-consistency barrier, so this
checkpoint makes incomplete provider state visible and retryable; physical
multi-device acceptance is still required.

# 2026-08-10 Build 159 automatic launcher/save-sync checkpoint

The maintainer clarified that iCloud save freshness is an app responsibility,
not a title-selection or manual-Settings workflow: reconciliation should begin
when Dark Eco opens to the Library, and every completed native save should be
uploaded automatically. Manual Sync remains available as an explicit retry,
but it is not the normal path.

Build 159 makes the Library lifecycle explicit. `GameLibraryView` calls
`SaveSyncController.launcherDidAppear()` when it becomes visible. Initial app
preparation delegates to the same idempotent entry point, and repeated SwiftUI
appearance callbacks share an already queued or active bidirectional operation
instead of producing concurrent or duplicate reconciliation. Returning from a
game or Game Setup to the Library therefore starts the same full reconciliation
before the player chooses a title.

The existing completed-frame detector remains the native-save hook. OpenGOAL's
memcard write is synchronous; after a successful game frame, Dark Eco schedules
a 250 ms coalesced stamp check off the display callback. A changed complete
bank pair enters upload-only reconciliation automatically. The frame never
waits for hashing, provider discovery, or iCloud I/O. Multiple writes within
the coalescing window converge on the newest closed generation.

New deterministic coverage proves the two automatic paths rather than relying
on source inspection:

- repeated Library appearances run exactly one active bidirectional operation;
- a completed local native generation uploads without any manual Sync action;
- scheduling the save check does not synchronously enter cloud I/O from the
  game frame;
- a deterministically newer iCloud generation remains untouched and visibly
  deferred for the next Library reconciliation.

Build 158's authoritative metadata discovery, upload-pending reporting,
pair-journal/CAS recovery, conflict preservation, and no-download-during-gameplay
contract remain unchanged. If the provider is still working when Play is tapped,
the existing bounded pregame safety gate may still finish that already-started
operation rather than risk booting an older local save; the operation now starts
at Library appearance instead of after title selection.

# 2026-08-10 Build 160 Modern V1 checkpoint

Build 160 adds the first bounded Modern graphics pass without adding another
profile selector. The existing Graphics **Modern / Classic** selector remains
the master. Modern exposes Filmic Color, Edge Smoothing, Clarity/Sharpening,
Soft Highlights, Vignette, and Film Grain as individual toggles, all enabled by
default. Classic sends an exact zero effect mask through the original Metal
present path while retaining the player's saved Modern choices. Restore
Defaults returns all six Modern effects to enabled.

The six-bit mask is persisted in the existing title settings document, flows
through Swift, Objective-C++, and the ordinary Metal host frame, and is applied
in the final present shader. The current work is deliberately a lightweight
single-pass presentation treatment. It does not claim replacement textures,
new geometry, multi-pass bloom, SSAO, LUT grading, or corrected stereo. Custom
texture import/selection and advanced Metal work are recorded as Planned in

# 2026-08-10 Build 161 stronger Modern V1 candidate

The maintainer physically tested Build 160 on Z iPad Pro and rejected its
Modern presentation: switching effects was effectively indistinguishable from
Classic except for slight dimming. This is a failed physical acceptance result,
not user uncertainty. The Build 160 proof only required at least one output
pixel to change by one byte and therefore established implementation wiring,
not useful perceptual separation.

Build 161 replaces that candidate with a stronger bounded presentation pass.
Filmic Color now uses a midpoint-preserving contrast curve and luma-relative
saturation instead of uniformly dimming nonwhite pixels. Edge Smoothing is
directional and edge-aware, Clarity uses thresholded local detail, Soft
Highlights has a meaningful bright-pass lift, and Vignette and Film Grain have
intentional but bounded strengths. All six still share the existing settings
bits and remain enabled by default under the existing **Modern / Classic**
master selector. No UI or persistence format changed. Classic still returns
the original shader expression before any Modern sampling or math.

The proof now measures changed content pixels, mean final-byte RGB delta, and
maximum channel delta per effect. It also checks that Filmic preserves neutral
midtone brightness and that the all-on defaults retain material separation at
1.5x output. The first stronger proof run failed five deliberately raised
thresholds, exposing fixture-local expectations and an insufficient highlight
pass. After narrowing local-effect coverage gates and strengthening the
bright-pass, the final full proof passed:

```text
zero-mask Classic: exact byte-for-byte match
Filmic: 39,936 pixels, mean changed-channel delta 7.44, max 11
Edge Smoothing: 272 edge pixels, mean 29.06, max 48
Clarity: 3,020 detail pixels, mean 5.65, max 19
Soft Highlights: 133,266 pixels, mean 1.20, max 24
Vignette: 84,827 pixels, mean 4.54, max 28
Film Grain: 191,767 pixels, mean 1.57, max 3
all-on at 1.5x: 473,940 pixels, mean 4.19, max 32
METAL PROOF PASSED
```

# 2026-08-10 Build 163 delayed iCloud save-convergence checkpoint

The maintainer's Build 162 two-device test reproduced the remaining false-
freshness path. Z iPhone Air initially exposed an older Jak 1 slot than Z iPad
Pro despite launch-time reconciliation and an app close/restart. Read-only,
explicitly authorized inspection of the two app-local save directories showed
that the iPhone's stale pair exactly matched its persisted sync baseline, while
the iPad's later pair and baseline matched each other. The iPhone later converged
without the newly installed iPad build being launched; afterward all seven
native banks and every pair baseline matched the iPad. No save bytes were added
to the repository.

This rules out corruption, a missing iPad upload, pair-journal failure, and save
generation parsing for the observed incident. The engine's bounded initial
metadata gather was correctly reconciling the provider inventory visible at
that moment, but `SaveSyncController` had no trigger when FileProvider exposed a
newer same-filename revision later. A launch or restart could therefore compare
the stale provider copy to the identical local copy, persist that identity, and
present `Up to date` before the provider caught up.

Build 163 closes that exact gap:

- One controller-owned `NSMetadataQuery` remains active for the private Jak 1
  saves subtree while save sync is enabled. `NSMetadataQueryDidUpdate` events
  feed the existing synchronization queue instead of replacing engine merge,
  pair-journal, hashing, or compare-and-swap authority.
- Provider events are debounced for 250 ms and duplicate events coalesce. Outside
  gameplay they enqueue bidirectional reconciliation. During gameplay they use
  the existing upload-only mode, so a provider event can never download into
  native gameplay storage.
- A pending provider-event debounce participates in the pregame gate. Play
  therefore cannot pass an already-observed newer provider revision before its
  reconciliation has completed or the existing bounded fallback has released
  cloud work safely.
- Disabling save sync stops the metadata monitor and cancels its pending event.
  Re-enabling, Library appearance, and iCloud identity changes restart it when
  the private container is available.
- A zero-transfer pass now says `No differences found in currently available
  iCloud saves` rather than making the globally unprovable claim `Up to date`.

The deterministic regression starts with identical synthetic generation-8,
85-percent local/cloud banks, finishes the first no-op reconcile, replaces the
same two cloud filenames with generation 10 at 90 percent without changing
their timestamps, and injects three provider-update notifications. Exactly one
follow-up reconcile runs, Play waits while it is suspended, both native banks
match the delayed cloud pair afterward, and the OpenGOAL loader selects
generation 10 at 90 percent. This test does not require an iCloud account or
retail data.

### Memory-pressure reclaim audit

`GameSession.handleMemoryWarning()` currently logs only. The smallest safe next
patch is to share one reclaimer between `.background` and memory warning: cancel
the already cancellation-safe foreground importer, wait any retained renderer
command to complete, release only the lazily recreated offscreen Metal color and
depth targets, and make readback fail cleanly until the next render recreates
them. `.inactive` should not purge for short interruptions.

Do not release or restart the kernel, EE/GOAL memory, memcards, save-sync state,
texture pool, wanted/common level art, Merc or bucket resources, PSO/sampler
caches, stream pages, distort snapshots, DMA copier cache, or runtime bridge.
Required deterministic coverage is: render/read/purge/no-read/idempotent
purge/re-render pixel parity in `metal-proof`; background and memory-warning
route ownership without kernel teardown; and the existing importer cancellation
fixture proving active install/candidate preservation and partial-only cleanup.

# 2026-08-12 Build 197 telemetry removal and DualSense rumble checkpoint

Build 197 removes all Build 196 in-game performance measurement after the
maintainer rejected the overlay and requested that no diagnostic work perturb

The physical DualSense report was weak overall and perceptible only on the right
side. The cause of the missing left/large response was a semantic mismatch: the
portable seam's `goal_pad_take_rumble` is an event latch, but the next frame's
zero immediately stopped the finite 120 ms Core Haptics player. Build 197 lets a
DualSense handle event finish that finite pulse. Explicit rumble disable,
lifecycle suspension, disconnect, and shutdown use a separate immediate silence
path. DualSense handle tuning also applies twofold clamped gain to the analog
right channel and distinct sharpness (low left, sharp right). This policy is
selected by the public `GCDualSenseGamepad` profile and only when both handle
localities exist. Other controllers and the default-locality fallback retain
their previous scale and zero behavior.

# 2026-08-12 Build 198 controller performance checkpoint

Build 198 removes two recent sources of controller-related main-thread churn
without changing renderer behavior, rumble gain, handle routing, or input
polling. The Build 186 finite Core Haptics path now reuses its standard pattern
player when intensity is unchanged instead of stopping and reconstructing the
event, pattern, and player every 80 ms. Apple documents that starting an
already-playing standard player restarts its pattern, so finite refresh and the
accepted DualSense pulse-tail behavior remain intact. Build 184's rapid-edge
callback now rejects thumbstick-only changes before dispatching to the main
queue; button, trigger, touchpad-button, and D-pad edges remain captured while
analog axes continue through per-frame polling.

Three independent read-only audits converged on Core Haptics churn as the
strongest post-Build-154 regression candidate and the unfiltered controller
callback as the second. They found no surviving Metal source change between the
accepted Build 154 renderer and Build 197. Older measurable candidates remain:
double FR3 decode/texture upload during level transitions, synchronous streamed
VAG reads, shipping renderer diagnostics, lazy PSO creation, the single
in-flight stream arena, 600-frame Swift diagnostics/logging, save stamp polling,

# 2026-08-12 Build 199 adaptive 120 Hz checkpoint

Build 199 adds an opt-in **High Frame Rate** setting that requests an adaptive
60–120 Hz iOS display-link range and captures one immutable 60/120 target for
each gameplay boot. The Objective-C++ seam supplies target-presentation timing
to the native runtime. Host-managed 120 Hz GOAL timing carries fractional
300 Hz and integral-frame remainders, ages controller history by elapsed virtual
frames, and keeps the established sound system on its 60 Hz vblank clock.

Direct per-callback high-FPS integrations use the immutable host cadence rather
than mutable gameplay slowdown. Counter conversions and fixed simulation steps

# 2026-08-12 Build 203 performance checkpoint

Build 203 layers four additional deterministic hot-path reductions on Build
202. This checkpoint remains unmeasured on physical hardware and does not claim
the adaptive 120 Hz goal is physically accepted.

Outer commits:

```text
5f84886f Eliminate input polling allocations (AI-assisted)
f3e76503 Reuse checked target state per frame (AI-assisted)
df9663cc Integrate asynchronous ocean composition (AI-assisted)
ed6d79e1 Skip unchanged input observation and haptic work (AI-assisted)
```

Controller polling now uses a fixed `UInt16` pressed mask plus `SIMD16<Float>`
values. The per-frame and rapid-edge paths share it. Keyboard/mouse reduction
has an empty fast path and one pass over its persistent held-control set instead
of transient filter/compactMap/Set collections. Exhaustive tests cover all
65,536 pressed masks for standard and remapped bindings, every control as an
analog L2/R2 owner, duplicate mappings, and opposing axes.

The native aggregate snapshot validates `*target*` once per successful frame
and reuses scalar current-state, next-state, look flags, and camera mode for
title, first-person, and speeder classification. Malformed current state, next
state, target type, declared size, and backing bounds remain independently
fail-closed. No GOAL object pointer persists across frames.

Nested OpenGOAL commit `a8cd0689c` removes up to two ocean-generation CPU/GPU
rendezvous on renderer-owned frames. The exact 33,792-byte dynamic ocean vertex
payload now lives in the frame stream. Ocean auxiliary buffers commit before
the tracked main frame on the same serial queue, whose completion guards stream
reuse; borrowed/headless paths retain their conservative wait.

Repeated silent rumble now consumes the native latch without publishing
observation or invoking haptic state. Sustained nonzero values still refresh
finite Core Haptics players, and the first zero transition still silences
ordinary controllers. Repeated unchanged button/stick values skip observable
writes.

# 2026-08-12 Build 204 performance checkpoint

Build 204 adds five bounded hot-path reductions on Build 203. It is signed and
simulator-launched, but remains unmeasured on physical hardware and does not
claim the adaptive 120 Hz goal is physically accepted.

Outer commits:


The GOALPad graphics host no longer scans the full DMA chain and copies every
referenced 128 KiB memory chunk before each synchronous render. The validated
live EE base and aligned root offset now remain call-scoped through ordinary,
stereo, direct, and ARM64 alternate-stack paths. The game and renderer still
share the same frame thread; DMA decoding completes before `host_send_chain`
returns, and boot/drop/thread/range guards remain fail-closed.

Generic2 reuses a fixed open-addressed draw-bucket lookup instead of allocating
an `unordered_map` for every active bucket. Static tfrag/tie/shrub level
textures are resolved once at load and cached beside their ownership handles,
removing a global registry mutex and hash lookup from normal background draws.
The missing-texture placeholder and handle-based unload paths remain intact.

The audio real-time callback now measures its exact peak while performing the
required stereo deinterleave instead of scanning the PCM a second time.
`framesRun` and `framesPresented` no longer invalidate Swift Observation every
frame; the opt-in diagnostics overlay receives a bounded revision every 60
successful game frames. GameController, keyboard, and mouse devices explicitly
deliver on their public main `handlerQueue`, so their callbacks update the
MainActor directly instead of enqueuing a redundant second main-queue block.

The host-managed OpenGOAL graphics menu no longer exposes its legacy frame-rate
row. More importantly, the central `set-frame-rate!` writer now retains the
host-reported immutable 60/120 target whenever the platform owns the display.
Late menu, speedrun, and debug writers therefore cannot split GOAL timing from
the Swift display link and native clock. Ordinary desktop OpenGOAL still uses
the requested rate, and PS2 behavior is untouched. The deterministic promotion
test now drives the real `DisplayClock` and `SoundFrameClock` for one second at
120/80/60/40/30 callbacks and proves 300 scaled ticks, 120 target-integral
units, 60 sound frames, the expected callback factors, one-shot pad-history
aging, and lifecycle sound-debt behavior.

The Metal Sprite renderer no longer destroys and recreates `std::map` nodes and
per-bucket vectors at every flush. One renderer owns an approximately 480 KiB
fixed 8,192-bucket pool, a 16,384-slot generation-reset lookup, and preallocated
linked sprite indices. First-use draw-bucket order and per-bucket encounter
order are preserved. The synthetic A/B/A texture proof exercises a reused
non-consecutive bucket and reads the exact expected pixel.

Native memcard code now publishes a `u64` generation only after a save bank is
fully written and `fclose` succeeds. That generation crosses the existing
fixed-size aggregate frame snapshot. Swift compares it by inequality, including
wraparound, and schedules the established 250 ms upload-only reconciliation
only for a real completed save. Ordinary game frames no longer construct a task
and later scan the save directory. Active work, bidirectional priority,
pregame gating, cancellation ownership, failure paths, kernel restart, and
shutdown behavior remain covered by the save and lifecycle suites.

With detailed developer diagnostics off, Metal no longer reads physical
`drawableID`, attaches an `addPresentedHandler`, or runs that callback's lock
and retained presentation-history scan every frame. The separate command-buffer
completion handler remains unconditional and continues to own GPU error
reporting, stream retirement/reuse, condition notification, and external stereo
completion. Generic desktop/proof callers retain detailed diagnostics by
default.

The existing rumble hot path already had the safe steady-zero coalescing from
`ed6d79e1`: enabled gameplay always consumes the native latch, repeated zero
skips observable/controller/device work, repeated nonzero still refreshes the
finite player, the first zero transition publishes, and explicit settings or
lifecycle cancellation is immediate. No additional rumble patch was made.

The current normal game target remains the established default 1280x960
internal render resolution (2x the 640x480 base, widened only when the selected
presentation aspect requires it), not the full Retina drawable. No speculative
dynamic-resolution change was made without a physical bottleneck trace.

# 2026-08-12 Build 206 frame-resource checkpoint

Build 206 removes the remaining source-proven CPU/GPU rendezvous in the
ordinary Metal frame path and one redundant Swift-to-Objective-C++ crossing.
It is signed and launched on the approved M5 simulator. No physical device was
accessed, and the adaptive-120 performance target is still not physically
accepted.

Outer commits after Build 205:

```text
0e491585 Fuse frame tick and state snapshot bridge
91ca0941 Integrate Build 206 performance checkpoint (AI-assisted)
4cb192ad Update performance source checks for Build 206 (AI-assisted)
```

Nested OpenGOAL commit after Build 205:

```text
036af5607 Ring Metal transient frame resources
```

The successful game tick now returns its post-tick fixed-size aggregate state
through the same Objective-C++ call. Swift no longer calls the bridge again
immediately after every successful frame. The original C++ and Objective-C
entry points remain for compatibility. A fused failure returns false with a
fully zeroed snapshot; success captures after `g_frames` advances, preserving
save-generation, exit, menu, look, prompt, and speeder ordering.

Ordinary layer-backed Metal frames now rotate through three exact-owned
resource slots. Each slot owns its transient stream pages and mutable
time-of-day/sky resources until that slot's exact command submission completes.
The first three frames therefore queue without the previous unconditional
one-frame CPU/GPU wait; the fourth waits only when wrapping to slot zero.
Borrowed/external stereo remains on a dedicated conservative fourth slot.
External completion is monotonic so a late callback from quarantined Vision
work cannot regress newer ownership. Completion/error reporting, external
busy/fallback behavior, same-queue eye/ocean auxiliary ordering, and exact
pixels remain unchanged.

Memory remains bounded. Ordinary gameplay can lazily allocate one 2 MiB stream
page in each of three slots (6 MiB total when all are used); the dedicated
external slot allocates separately only when that path is used. Time-of-day
palettes add three 32 KiB copies, or 96 KiB per loaded tfrag/tie/shrub tree.
Sky slot copies add approximately 60 KiB in total. No real FR3 was available
to measure the aggregate loaded-level count.

The audio Player lock was audited but not changed. An optimized host probe with
48 permanent silent voices measured nominal `Tick(480)` at 27.7 us median,
39.0 us p99, and 84.5 us maximum. The mutex can starve a command under an
artificial continuous-reacquisition loop, but safely replacing it requires a
larger command/ownership redesign. No `try_lock`, dropped command, PCM, pause,
bank, or lifecycle behavior was changed. Probe artifacts:

## Build 207 adaptive 24 Hz fallback checkpoint (2026-08-12)

Build 207 closes one source-proven correctness gap in the experimental High
Frame Rate path. Apple's adaptive display cadence can fall to 24 Hz despite a
requested 60-120 Hz range. Build 206 capped the host display-time ratio at four,
which would advance only 96 of 120 target-frame units and 48 of 60 sound frames
per sustained 24 Hz second. Build 207 permits ratio five only for the
PC-host-managed 120 Hz timing domain. The accepted 60 Hz path, ordinary desktop
OpenGOAL, and PS2 retain their existing cap and behavior.

The same narrow gate now permits five controller-history steps. Deterministic
coverage proves 120, 80, 60, 48, 40, 30, and 24 Hz all advance 300 scaled
ticks, 120 target integral units, and 60 sound frames per wall-clock second;
the 24 Hz sound trace alternates two and three frames, and a relative input edge
ages into the fifth existing history slot without duplication.

### Build 207 physical performance capture workflow

Outer commit `d6fac383` (`Add physical ProMotion capture workflow
(AI-assisted)`) makes the remaining physical gate reproducible without adding
shipping runtime instrumentation. `Scripts/capture-ios-game-performance.sh`
requires explicit `--device`, `--mode`, `--kind`, and `--output` arguments. It
does not enumerate devices, install, or launch the app. The signed app must
already be running at the prepared route; the helper attaches `xctrace`, records
one Game Performance Overview, Metal System Trace, Time Profiler, or Power
Profiler run, exports its table of contents, and records exact outer/nested
commits and capture metadata. `--dry-run` performs no device access.

`docs/BUILDING.md` now defines a counterbalanced warmed Spider Cave protocol:
60-A, HFR-A, HFR-B, then 60-B with Developer Logs off, Low Power Mode off, fixed
graphics/resolution/input/route/brightness, and matching nominal starting
thermal state. Each settings change requires a new gameplay session because the
60/120 target is immutable for a session. Short overview/Metal/CPU runs default
to 30 seconds; the sustained Power Profiler run defaults to five minutes. Judge
the result against actual adaptive cadence, including its corresponding frame
budget, rather than requiring continuous 120 Hz. HFR must enter a cadence above
60 Hz in the warmed route without recurring multi-interval hitches or a worse
60 Hz baseline. Camera/timer/audio, input, saves, and rumble remain acceptance
requirements.

### Build 207 deterministic trace analysis checkpoint

Outer commit `cd66fc02` (`Add deterministic iOS performance trace analyzer`)

tables from an existing `.trace`, but never records, enumerates, launches, or

deterministic `report.json` plus compact `report.csv`.

The parser preserves xctrace's distinct raw, formatted, and element-type values
through `id`/`ref` references. Duration and Time Profiler weight values are
normalized only from supported raw nanosecond payloads; unsupported units fail
closed instead of being reported as milliseconds. Process, metric, thermal,
and stack identities use their formatted display values, and measurement rows
are restricted to `Dark Eco`. The first run exposes a deterministic
`metric_catalog` so exact observed metric names/labels can be selected without
guessing. Cadence reports include 120/80/60/48/40/30/24 clusters and contiguous
runs. Threshold crossings are explicitly `multi_interval_hitch_candidates`,
because a sustained adaptive ProMotion downshift is not by itself a hitch.

### Build 207 counterbalanced comparison checkpoint

Outer commit `63c76bcb` (`Add offline iOS performance run comparator`) upgrades
the per-run report to schema v2 and adds
`Scripts/compare-ios-game-performance.py`. This remains non-shipping tooling;
it reads four completed reports and never records, enumerates, launches, or
contacts a device.

The schema retains an exact nanosecond interval histogram, total and per-cadence
durations, contiguous cadence-run durations, duration- and sample-weighted
above-60-Hz shares, candidate counts at 1.5x/2x/3x, exact selected metric source
identity, thermal state summaries, a versioned analysis contract, and an
explicit operator-supplied run context. Runtime settings are never inferred.
The context requires the route, graphics profile, resolution, input,
brightness, Low Power Mode off, Developer Logs off, nominal initial thermal
state, run label, and an independently verified installed-build identity.

The comparator accepts exactly `60-A`, `HFR-A`, `HFR-B`, and `60-B`. It fails
closed on mismatched device, source heads, installed build, process, mode,
template/kind, requested or actual duration, xctrace version, analysis
contract, controlled settings, cadence metric identity/units, candidate
semantics, or thermal coverage. It independently reconstructs cadence clusters,
duration totals, above-60 evidence, percentiles, runs, and candidate thresholds
from each exact histogram. Thermal intervals must be ordered, non-overlapping,
effectively contiguous, cover the trace, match the operator-declared start, and
start equivalently within the adjacent counterbalanced pairs
`60-A`/`HFR-A` and `HFR-B`/`60-B`.

Output keeps the two different weighting questions explicit: sample share and
wall-time duration share. HFR evidence means any classified cadence above
60 Hz in both HFR replicates; it does not require a 120 Hz cluster. Exact
sample-weighted pooled percentiles and equal-replicate median-of-run summaries
are both labeled. Threshold crossings remain candidates, never an automatic
hitch or performance-acceptance verdict. Camera/timer/audio/input/save/rumble
and sustained power evidence remain manual or separate capture gates.
